title: Education Lein, Jo Too Much Future
author: Lein, Jo
summary: The author, a teacher who recovered from alcoholism, uses her personal recovery experience to illuminate why struggling students shut down rather than engage with overwhelming goals. Her central insight -- 'there's too much future' -- names the mechanism: when the gap between where a person is and where they need to be feels infinite, they don't try harder, they disengage. In recovery, the 'next right thing' philosophy provided a framework that transferred directly to working with students who carry accumulated academic deficits. The article argues that educators routinely mistake the need for a larger vision when struggling people actually need a smaller, more immediate one. Evidence of capability accumulates through tiny sequential actions, and that evidence -- not motivation -- is what slowly produces belief. The reframe has direct classroom application: instead of pointing students toward graduation or the end of the year, teachers can offer one paragraph, one problem, one next right thing.
points: * Struggling students don't resist goals -- they resist impossibility: when people cannot imagine success, they shut down, detach, or surrender rather than try harder, and educators who mistake this disbelief for defiance respond with the wrong intervention. * The 'too much future' pattern in recovery mirrors the pattern in classrooms: overwhelming someone with the full scope of what they need to accomplish creates paralysis, not motivation, and the cure is a shorter horizon, not a larger vision. * Tiny actions build evidence, and evidence builds belief: a sponsor's job was not to get the author sober but to help her prove she could do one thing, then another -- and this incremental proof-of-capability is the mechanism that makes change possible. * The Backfire Effect explains why confronting a struggling person with evidence of the problem makes it worse -- the more evidence is presented, the more the person defends the behavior that is destroying them. * A blank page in front of a struggling kid is not a blank page -- it is every blank page every adult has ever handed them; by the time today's assignment arrives, the student is already carrying a mountain.
quotes: When my family first confronted me about my drinking, I doubled down. The Backfire Effect in action. The more evidence people presented, the more I defended the thing that was actively destroying me.
We often mistake disbelief for defiance. But when people cannot imagine success, they don't usually try harder. They shut down. They detach. They surrender.
I wasn't carrying a drinking problem. I was carrying too much future. Every conversation about recovery felt like a conversation about forever.
Looking back, my temporary sponsor wasn't helping me get sober. He was helping me prove that I could do one thing. Then another. Then another.
I think educators make this mistake all the time. We assume struggling people need a bigger vision. Sometimes they need a smaller one.
People see laziness. I don't. Sometimes that kid isn't looking at a blank page. They're looking at every adult who has ever handed them another blank page.
Struggling people don't need forever. They need five minutes. One paragraph. One problem. One class period. One meeting. One dollar. One next right thing.
